text: David Hanson Jr. is an American roboticist and the founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Hanson Robotics, a Hong Kong–based robotics company established in 2013. He specializes in designing human-looking robots with realistic facial expressions, including Sophia, which became the world's first robot to be granted citizenship and has received widespread media attention. Born on December 20, 1969, in Dallas, Texas, Hanson attended Highland Park High School for his senior year to focus on math and science. As a teenager, he enjoyed drawing and reading science fiction by Isaac Asimov and Philip K. Dick, the latter of whom he later replicated in android form. Hanson holds a Bachelor of Fine Arts from the Rhode Island School of Design in Film, Animation, Video (FAV) and a Ph.D. from the University of Texas at Dallas in interactive arts and engineering. In 1995, as part of an independent-study project on out-of-body experiences, he built a humanoid head in his own likeness operated by a remote operator. In 2004, at a Denver American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) conference, Hanson presented K-Bot, a robotic head with polymer skin, finely sculpted features, and big blue eyes, named after his lab assistant Kristen Nelson; it featured 24 servomotors and cameras in its eyes, and he was 33 years old at the time, a graduate student at the University of Texas at Dallas. After graduating, Hanson worked as an artist and later joined Disney as a sculptor and material researcher in the Disney Imagineering Lab, and also worked as a designer, sculptor, and robotics developer for Universal Studios and MTV. In 2004, he built Hertz, a female animated robot head that took nine months to construct. Hanson has published in journals covering materials science, artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and robotics. He believes precise human appearances are essential for effective human-robot communication and that social humanoid robots can serve humanity in roles such as tutor, companion, or security guard. He also argues that the realism of his robots may pose an "identity challenge to the human being" and could polarize audiences between those who appreciate realism and those who find it disturbing. Many of his robots are currently used in research or non-profit settings at institutions such as the University of Cambridge, University of Geneva, University of Pisa, and cognitive science and AI laboratories. Zeno, a two-foot-tall cartoon-style robot, provides treatment sessions for children with autism through a collaboration involving the University of Texas at Arlington, Dallas Autism Treatment Center, Texas Instruments, National Instruments, and Hanson. Other creations include Albert Einstein HUBO, a robotic head resembling Albert Einstein mounted on a HUBO bipedal frame, and Professor Einstein, a 14.5-inch personal robot that engages in conversation and serves as a companion or tutor. Hanson collaborated with musician David Byrne on Song for Julio, which was exhibited at the Reina Sofia Museum in Madrid in 2008 as part of the Máquinas&Almas (Souls&Machines) exhibit, and his robots have since appeared in museums worldwide. From 2011 to 2013, he served as an adjunct professor of Computer Science and Engineering Teaching at the University of Texas at Arlington; he also taught in 2010 at the University of North Texas in fine arts, kinetic/interactive sculpture, and at the University of Texas at Dallas as an instructor in interactive sculpture. Hanson delivers keynote speeches at major international technology conferences, including the Consumer Electronics Show and IBC.
